messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Kai still sees the night his ex-boyfriend’s hands closed around his throat—but only in fragments. Because the memory came back so vividly, he began to see threads of it everywhere: in strangers' faces, in certain times of day, in the quality of winter light. Because the memory returned so vividly in pieces, he began to see threats everywhere — every shadow at dusk, every abrupt silence in the apartment, every unexpected touch felt like the start of the same story. Already running on threat, he found that almost anything could tip into a warning — a van parked at an odd angle, a light left on that shouldn't have been. Some moments are impossibly sharp, like the pressure against his windpipe, while others are blank, and he can never quite piece the order together. That confused sequence has left him with a quiet certainty that the event happened because of who he is, that he is fundamentally inadequate, that he no longer belongs anywhere. Once he had concluded that he didn’t belong anywhere, almost anything could confirm it — a closed door in his studio, a conversation that turned quiet when he entered, the way a stranger’s gaze lingered a second too long. As a painter, these thoughts follow him into his studio, where the silence of an empty room makes him feel watched. The faint creak of a floorboard floods him with unwanted thoughts of footsteps approaching, and he finds himself scanning for exits—the fire escape, the back door—even when he knows he is alone.

The uncertainty that now colors everything has become a trigger of its own. If a canvas takes longer to dry than expected, Kai assumes something bad is happening, and that feeling of nameless threat sends him straight back into the memory of being trapped, reliving the helplessness as if it is happening right now. To cope, he has started freezing completely when he feels threatened—a strategy that once, during a minor argument with his current partner, made him stand motionless in the kitchen for nearly a minute, unable to speak. His own habit of freezing had turned the kitchen counter, the angle of the afternoon light, even the smell of cooking onions into reminders that could trigger the same paralysis again. The freeze itself deepens his sense of inadequacy: he is not the sort of person who should be in a relationship. He avoids anything that reminds him of his ex—certain songs, neighborhoods, the way someone stands too close—but the avoidance only sharpens the partial clarity of what happened, because he is constantly on guard against reminders.

Kai has also begun to avoid sleeping during the times of day when nightmares tend to come, usually late afternoon when the light slants the same way it did on that afternoon. He listens for sounds that might mean someone is entering his home—the lock clicking, a floorboard shifting. That hypervigilance makes the memories feel even more real, as if the danger is still present. Living at that pitch of alertness, he found ordinary cues had become warnings — the mail slot rattling, a car door slamming outside, the hum of a ceiling fan — each one confirming what his body already believed. And when a delayed delivery or a slow text message from his partner triggers that deep uncertainty, the threat feels confirmed: something bad is coming, and it is his fault for being the sort of person this happens to.

In his work, he used to paint large, confident abstracts; now he finds himself working in a small corner of the studio, back to the wall, facing the door. The scanning for exits has become automatic, and he rarely finishes a piece because he cannot tolerate the feeling of someone watching him—even if no one is there. His partner has noticed the changes, the way he flinches at unexpected touches, the way he shuts down when plans change. Kai knows he is pushing his partner away, but the thought of belonging nowhere feels like a truth he cannot argue with.

What finally brought him to seek help was a moment of freezing in the middle of a gallery opening—his own solo show—when a stranger brushed against his shoulder and the reliving seared through him so vividly that he dropped a glass. He stood there, unable to move, while the crowd blurred. That night he made the appointment. He is afraid of being seen as broken, but he is more afraid of staying stuck in a loop where every trigger leads to threat, every memory strengthens his self-blame, and every strategy he uses only tightens the trap.
